lesson.title: Slicing the Shell: Understanding Subshells
lesson.summary: Each principal energy level is divided into subshells, labeled s, p, d, and f, which differ in shape and in how many electrons they can hold, refining the picture set up by the principal quantum number.
lesson.body:
The principal quantum number, n, identifies which main shell an electron belongs to and sets the maximum number of electrons that shell can hold, using the formula 2n^2. But except for the very simplest case, the n=1 shell, every shell is not a single uniform region; it is divided into smaller groups of orbitals called subshells, each with its own characteristic shape and slightly different energy. Understanding subshells fills in the internal structure that the principal quantum number alone leaves unexplained.

Subshells are labeled with letters, s, p, d, and f, and the number of subshells present within a given shell equals the value of n for that shell. The n=1 shell has only one subshell, the 1s. The n=2 shell has two subshells, 2s and 2p. The n=3 shell has three subshells, 3s, 3p, and 3d. The n=4 shell has four subshells, 4s, 4p, 4d, and 4f. Each type of subshell is built from a specific number of individual orbitals, and each orbital, regardless of subshell type, can hold a maximum of two electrons. An s subshell contains 1 orbital, holding up to 2 electrons total. A p subshell contains 3 orbitals, holding up to 6 electrons total. A d subshell contains 5 orbitals, holding up to 10 electrons total. An f subshell contains 7 orbitals, holding up to 14 electrons total.

This is exactly the detail that explains where the 2n^2 formula for shell capacity comes from. Take the n=3 shell as a worked example. It contains three subshells: 3s, 3p, and 3d. The 3s subshell holds up to 2 electrons, the 3p subshell holds up to 6 electrons, and the 3d subshell holds up to 10 electrons. Adding these together gives 2 + 6 + 10 = 18 electrons total for the n=3 shell, which matches exactly the value predicted by 2n^2 = 2(3)^2 = 18. The principal quantum number's capacity formula and the subshell-by-subshell count are two ways of arriving at the same answer, and seeing them agree is a good confirmation that both ideas are being applied correctly.

Subshells also differ from one another in shape, which affects how their electrons are distributed in space around the nucleus. An s orbital is spherical, centered symmetrically on the nucleus. A p orbital has a dumbbell shape, with two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus, and there are three p orbitals per p subshell, oriented along three perpendicular directions. The d and f orbitals have more complex, multi-lobed shapes. These shapes are not arbitrary artistic choices; they come directly from solving the quantum mechanical equations that describe each orbital's probability distribution.

Subshells matter beyond bookkeeping because the order in which they fill with electrons, and the specific number of electrons in an atom's outermost subshells, governs how that atom bonds with other atoms and where it sits in the periodic table. The s, p, d, and f block regions of the periodic table are named directly after which type of subshell is being filled by the outermost electrons of the elements in that region. Every subshell discussed here builds directly on the principal quantum number that identifies its shell, which in turn builds on the energy levels and quantum mechanical model that established why electrons are restricted to these specific, describable regions in the first place.
